claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution in five-or-more-metal near-equimolar nanoparticles across 473–1923 K.
Sluggish atomic diffusion at intermediate temperatures helps the nanoparticles retain their single-phase structure.
Moderate enthalpic driving forces are insufficient to overcome entropy stabilization and cause significant segregation or a phase transition under the stated conditions.
The starting material is an as-synthesized, equimolar or near-equimolar nanoparticle containing at least five metals and confirmed to be a single-phase solid solution.
The proposed intervention is in-situ heating from 473 K to 1923 K under inert and catalytic atmospheres while monitoring structure and composition.
The heating protocol uses controlled ramps and dwell steps in vacuum or reactive-gas flow.
Increasing temperature amplifies the configurational-entropy contribution to the free-energy balance.
The increased entropy contribution suppresses large-scale compositional demixing.
Reduced diffusion at intermediate temperatures kinetically impedes phase separation.
After thermal cycling between 473 K and 1923 K, the nanoparticles will remain predominantly single-phase relative to their initial state.
Thermal cycling over 473–1923 K will produce minimal compositional segregation.
Thermal cycling over 473–1923 K will produce minimal lattice transformation.
Above approximately 1923 K, enthalpic contributions may dominate and cause phase transitions or segregation.
Large deviations from near-equimolar composition may allow enthalpic contributions to dominate and cause phase transitions or segregation.
Comparative data are limited at the highest temperatures and across varying gas partial pressures.
Persistent secondary phases or elemental segregation beyond measurement error would falsify the proposed stabilization mechanism.
